title: TS SDK: zipper stream unifier for async-iterator & Web Streams interop
creator: Priya Patel
description:
Problem: TypeScript SDK customers mix consumer patterns: some prefer async iterators (for for-await loops), others prefer Web Streams (ReadableStream) for browser-native plumbing. Existing bridge primitives focus on one-way adapters and checkpoint/resume semantics. We are seeing edge cases where combining two independent sources (tokens + metadata, or primary + sideband) needs a deterministic interleave while preserving backpressure, cancellation, and retry semantics across both consumption models.

Goal: Implement a 'zipper' stream unifier primitive in the TS SDK that can take N source producers (async-iterables or ReadableStreams) and yield a single unified output stream in both async-iterator and ReadableStream forms. The zipper should: 1) preserve backpressure semantics when the caller uses either consumption model, 2) propagate cancellation from either side to the underlying producers, 3) implement configurable alignment strategies (strict-pair, first-wins, timestamp-merge), 4) surface deterministic error semantics and offer retry hooks for transient producer failures.

Non-goals: This ticket does not implement server-side changes to the API surface (no protocol changes). We will implement the primitive inside the SDK and use it in examples and internal playgrounds.

Success metrics: SDK integration tests exercising interop pass, latency regression < 3% on our micro-benchmarks, and an example README demonstrating both consumption patterns is published.
acceptance_criteria: Provide a documented TypeScript API: zipper(sources, options) -> { asyncIterator: AsyncIterable, webStream: ReadableStream }
Backpressure map: when the consumer awaits next() or calls getReader().read(), producers should only be advanced when there is demand
Cancellation propagation: calling return() on the async iterator or cancel() on the ReadableStream should cancel all underlying sources and call provided onCancel hooks
Three alignment strategies implemented and covered by unit tests: strict-pair, first-wins, timestamp-merge
Clear error semantics: aggregated errors vs short-circuiting are configurable and documented
Integration examples: two sample apps in examples/ts/ demonstrating token+metadata merge and audio+transcript merge
E2E interop tests: consume unified stream as for-await and as ReadableStream and assert identical logical output sequences
Performance: micro-benchmark included showing memory < 25MB and CPU < 3% overhead vs raw async iterator baseline
PR merged and a canary published (npm tag: rc-zipper) for internal teams to try
technical_notes: API shape: zipper<S>(sources: Array<AsyncIterable<S>|ReadableStream<S>>, opts?: ZipperOpts) -> { asyncIterator: AsyncIterable<UnifiedEvent>, webStream: ReadableStream<UnifiedEvent> }
Internal model: per-source ring buffer + demand tokens. A unified scheduler polls sources only when global demand > 0. This maps iterator.next() and reader.read() to the same demand counter.

Backpressure: use a single Atomic demand counter (JS number guarded by queue) with Promise resolvers to wake producers. For browser environments where atomics not available, fall back to microtask-based signaling.
Cancellation: expose registerCancel callbacks from sources; zipper will call them and then await their completion with a short timeout to avoid hang in edge-case producers.

Retries: zipper accepts onError hook returning a RetryDecision { retry: boolean, delayMs?: number, transform?: (item) => item }. We'll plumb this to SDK's existing retry utilities to reuse jitter/backoff logic.
Memory: implement bounded per-source buffers (configurable, default 8 items) and backpressure propagation upstream when full.

Edge cases: when a source ends early, alignment strategy determines behavior: strict-pair -> close zipper with error if pair incomplete; first-wins -> emit remaining items; timestamp-merge -> emit remaining with order by timestamp metadata.
Types: provide robust generics so zipper preserves item typings and carries optional sideband metadata like {sourceId, seq, ts}.
Interop: webStream is implemented via new ReadableStream({ start, pull, cancel }) where pull increments demand and start wires producers. For Node, use web-streams-polyfill where needed.
implementation_plan: WIP branch: feat/ts-zipper-unifier (forked from main) - link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-sdk/compare/main...feat/ts-zipper-unifier
Step 1: Package-level API and types (lib/streams/zipper.ts) - create initial tests for API shape
Step 2: Implement scheduler & per-source buffers; unit tests for backpressure mapping
Step 3: Add alignment strategies and retry hooks; fuzz tests with synthetic producers
Step 4: Implement ReadableStream wrapper and Node/browser integration shims
Step 5: Examples and playground app (examples/zipper-token-metadata and examples/audio-transcript)
Step 6: Performance micro-benchmark and CI perf job
Step 7: PR review, address security checklist, publish rc-zipper npm tag

testing_plan: Unit tests: per-source buffer edge cases, alignment mode permutations, cancellation semantics (return()/cancel()).
Integration tests: spin up two synthetic producers (fast/slow) and consume as for-await and via ReadableStream.getReader(), assert consistent output
Fuzz tests: random delays, random source termination ordering, transient errors with onError decisions - assert no resource leak
Perf tests: Micro-benchmark comparing zipper vs baseline async iterator for single-source and two-source cases with 1k items
Browser matrix: test in Chromium and Safari for ReadableStream behavior. Use Playwright job in CI.
Canary usage: push npm rc tag and ask internal teams (Console, Examples) to try and report issues within 2 weeks.
risks: Complexity in mapping demand between two consumption models can introduce subtle race conditions; careful unit tests and timeouts are required.
Polyfill behavior differences between Node and browsers (reader.read() timing) could cause unexpected buffering. We will detect via CI matrix.
Retries combined with strict-pair alignment may cause head-of-line blocking; document trade-offs and provide options to tune timeouts.
If the primitive leaks Promises from producers during abrupt cancellation, long-lived resource leaks could occur. Add leak detector to CI (open handles check).
notes: Design discussion: prefer explicit api over implicit cast-to-webstream to avoid surprising GC/cancellation semantics.
Follow-up: consider adding Python and Go port stubs if pattern proves useful across SDKs.
